courses.name: ECON 203 · Introduction to Macroeconomics
courses.description: Concordia ECON 203 (Ragan, Macroeconomics, 18th Canadian ed.): key macro variables, national income accounting, the Keynesian AE model and multipliers, AD/AS and factor-price adjustment, long-run growth, money and banking, Bank of Canada monetary policy, inflation and the NAIRU, government debt, exchange rates and the balance of payments. Chapters without slides yet are tagged 'ahead'.

topics.name: Real vs Nominal GDP & the Deflator
Multiplier with Taxes & Imports; Fiscal Policy
Real GDP & the Price Level in the Short Run (Ch. 8)
From the Short Run to the Long Run (Ch. 9)

items.prompt: National income measured in current dollars is **{{c1::nominal}}** national income; measured in constant (base-period) dollars it is **{{c2::real}}** national income.
items.explanation: Real national income changes only when *quantities* change; nominal income also moves when prices change.

items.prompt: **Potential output** ($Y^*$) is the level of real GDP the economy would produce if all productive resources were {{c1::fully employed}}.
items.explanation: $Y^*$ is not a maximum: some unemployment (frictional and structural) still exists at $Y^*$. It is the 'normal capacity' level that actual output fluctuates around.

items.prompt: The **output gap** is $\text{Output gap} = {{c1::Y - Y^*}}$, actual output minus potential output.
items.explanation: Sign convention matters: a *negative* gap means output is below potential (recessionary); a *positive* gap means output is above potential (inflationary).

items.prompt: If $Y < Y^*$ the economy has which kind of gap? And if $Y > Y^*$?
items.answer: $Y < Y^*$: a **recessionary gap**. $Y > Y^*$: an **inflationary gap**.
items.explanation: Below potential, resources are idle and output is lost (recession). Above potential, factor markets are over-stretched, which pushes wages and prices up (inflation).

items.prompt: Name the four phases of the business cycle in order, starting from the bottom.
items.answer: Trough, recovery, peak, recession.
items.explanation: Real GDP shows a clear positive long-run trend (almost 300% growth since 1975) with short-term fluctuations around it; the cycle describes those fluctuations.

items.prompt: Most macroeconomic issues fall into which two categories, and which one matters more for generation-to-generation living standards?
items.answer: Long-run trends (growth) and short-run fluctuations (business cycles). Long-term growth matters more for living standards across generations, though it gets less media attention.
items.explanation: Economists debate how much policy can affect long-run growth, and whether governments should try to 'fine-tune' short-run fluctuations with frequent spending and tax changes.

items.prompt: The **labour force** is everyone employed or unemployed: $LF = {{c1::E + U}}$.
items.explanation: People who are neither working nor looking for work (students, retirees, discouraged workers) are *not* in the labour force, so they do not count as unemployed.

items.prompt: The **unemployment rate** is $u = \dfrac{{{c1::U}}}{{{c2::LF}}} \times 100$ (unemployed as a percentage of the labour force).
items.explanation: Example: 1.2 million unemployed in a labour force of 20 million gives $u = 6\%$. Dividing by the whole population would be a classic mistake.

items.prompt: How is the **labour force participation rate** defined?
items.answer: The labour force as a percentage of the working-age population (in Canada, people aged 15 and over).
items.explanation: $\text{Participation rate} = \dfrac{LF}{\text{Working-age population}} \times 100$. It can fall when discouraged workers stop searching, which lowers the measured unemployment rate without anyone finding a job.

items.prompt: Is the unemployment rate zero when the economy is at potential output $Y^*$? Why or why not?
items.answer: No. At $Y^*$ (full employment) there is still **frictional** unemployment (normal labour-market turnover) and **structural** unemployment (mismatch between jobs and workers).
items.explanation: Full employment means zero *cyclical* unemployment, not zero unemployment.

items.prompt: Distinguish frictional, structural and cyclical unemployment.
items.answer: **Frictional**: normal turnover as people move between jobs. **Structural**: mismatch between the skills/location of workers and available jobs. **Cyclical**: extra unemployment when $Y < Y^*$.
items.explanation: Frictional and structural exist even at $Y^*$; cyclical unemployment is positive only during a recessionary gap.

items.prompt: **Labour productivity** $= \dfrac{\text{Real GDP}}{{{c1::\text{Employment (or total hours worked)}}}}$; productivity growth is the single largest cause of rising {{c2::material living standards}} over long periods.
items.explanation: Productivity in general is output per unit of input; labour productivity picks labour as the input.

items.prompt: The **price level** is the average level of all prices in the economy expressed as an {{c1::index number}}; **inflation** is the {{c2::percentage change}} in the price level from one period to the next.
items.explanation: The most used measure for calculating inflation is the Consumer Price Index (CPI).

items.prompt: Inflation rate from a price index: $\pi = \dfrac{{{c1::P_t - P_{t-1}}}}{{{c2::P_{t-1}}}} \times 100$
items.explanation: Example: CPI goes from 125 to 130, so $\pi = \frac{5}{125} \times 100 = 4\%$. Divide by the *earlier* level, not the later one.

items.prompt: What does inflation do to the purchasing power of money and to sums fixed in nominal terms?
items.answer: It reduces the purchasing power of money and reduces the real value of any sum fixed in nominal (dollar) terms, such as a fixed pension or a loan.
items.explanation: We value money for what it buys; purchasing power is the amount of goods and services one unit of money can buy.

items.prompt: Why does *unanticipated* inflation matter more than fully anticipated inflation?
items.answer: If inflation is fully anticipated, households and firms adjust nominal prices and wages to keep their real values; unanticipated inflation changes real values and redistributes.
items.explanation: In practice inflation is rarely fully anticipated or fully unanticipated, so some but not all adjustments are made and the allocation of resources is affected.

items.prompt: The **real interest rate** equals the nominal interest rate {{c1::minus the inflation rate}}.
items.explanation: Example: nominal rate 6% with 4% inflation gives a real rate of 2%. The real rate is the return adjusted for the change in the purchasing power of money.

items.prompt: The **bank rate** is the rate the {{c1::Bank of Canada}} charges on short-term loans to commercial banks; the **prime rate** is the rate banks charge their {{c2::best customers}}.
If inflation rises while the nominal interest rate stays fixed, what happens to the real interest rate and to borrowers?
items.answer: The real interest rate falls; borrowers repay in money that buys less, so they gain at the lender's expense.
items.explanation: Real rate $= i - \pi$: higher $\pi$ with fixed $i$ means a lower real rate. This is why unanticipated inflation redistributes from lenders to borrowers.

items.prompt: The **exchange rate** is the amount of one currency needed to purchase one unit of another; in this course it is units of {{c1::domestic currency (C\$)}} per unit of {{c2::foreign currency}}.
items.explanation: January 2024: 1 euro cost 1.47 Canadian dollars, so the C\$/euro exchange rate was 1.47. The slide's appreciation/depreciation definition fixes the direction: C\$ *per* unit of foreign money, not the reverse.

items.prompt: Under the course's definition of the exchange rate, is an **appreciation** of the Canadian dollar a rise or a fall in the exchange rate?
items.answer: A **fall**: it takes *fewer* Canadian dollars to buy one unit of foreign currency. A depreciation is a *rise* in the exchange rate.
items.explanation: Counter-intuitive but exam-critical. If the C\$/US\$ rate goes from 1.35 to 1.30, the C\$ has appreciated.

items.prompt: **Net exports** (the **trade balance**) $= {{c1::\text{exports} - \text{imports}}}$, written $NX = X - IM$.
items.explanation: Canada's exports and imports have grown closely in step, so the trade balance has stayed relatively small as a share of GDP.

items.prompt: Why would adding up the sales of *all* firms overstate national output?
items.answer: Double counting: production occurs in stages, so intermediate goods sold between firms would be counted again inside the price of the final good.
items.explanation: Only **final goods** (sold for consumption, investment, government or export in the period) should be counted.

items.prompt: Intermediate good vs final good?
items.answer: **Intermediate**: output used as an input by another firm. **Final**: not used as an input by other firms; produced to be sold for consumption, investment, government or export in the period.
items.explanation: The same physical good can be either: flour sold to a bakery is intermediate; flour sold to a household is final.

items.prompt: $\text{Value added} = \text{Sales revenue} - {{c1::\text{Cost of intermediate goods}}}$, which also equals the {{c2::payments owed to the firm's factors of production}}.
items.explanation: Summing value added across all firms avoids double counting and gives GDP.

items.prompt: A mining company sells ore for \$1000, a steel producer turns it into steel sold for \$1500, and a fabricator sells the metal product for \$1800. What is total value added?
items.answer: \$1800: $1000 + 500 + 300$. Total sales would be \$4300, but \$2500 of that is interfirm sales of intermediate goods.
items.explanation: Value added equals the value of the final product (\$1800), which is also the sum of all payments to factors of production.

items.prompt: Three ways of measuring national income, all yielding GDP: sum all {{c1::value added}}, sum all {{c2::expenditure on final domestic output}}, or sum all {{c3::income generated by domestic production}}.
items.explanation: GDP is the total market value of all final goods and services produced in an economy during a given period. In practice a *statistical discrepancy* reconciles the measures.

items.prompt: Expenditure side (actual values, subscript $a$): $GDP = C_a + I_a + G_a + {{c1::NX_a}}$, where $NX_a = X_a - IM_a$.
items.explanation: Consumption + investment + government purchases + net exports. Imports are subtracted because they were counted inside $C$, $I$ and $G$ but were not produced here.

items.prompt: What three things make up investment expenditure ($I$) in GDP?
items.answer: Changes in inventories, additions to plant and equipment, and new residential housing construction.
items.explanation: Investment is expenditure on goods *not for present consumption*. Buying shares or bonds is not investment in the GDP sense.

items.prompt: $\text{Net investment} = \text{Gross investment} - {{c1::\text{Depreciation}}}$
items.explanation: Gross investment creates new capital goods (fixed investment); depreciation is the part of output that merely replaces worn-out capital, so net investment is the actual change in the capital stock.

items.prompt: Are government transfer payments (e.g., Old Age Security, EI benefits) included in $G$?
items.answer: No. $G$ is government purchases of *currently produced* goods and services only; transfers are excluded because nothing is produced in exchange.
items.explanation: Transfers reappear in GDP only when the recipient spends them (as $C$).

items.prompt: A Canadian household buys a \$30,000 car made in Germany. What happens to Canadian GDP?
items.answer: Nothing: $C$ rises by \$30,000 and $IM$ rises by \$30,000, so $C + I + G + (X - IM)$ is unchanged.
items.explanation: That is the whole point of subtracting imports: to leave only spending on *domestically produced* output.

items.prompt: From the income side, GDP is the sum of which three groups of items?
items.answer: Factor incomes (wages and salaries, interest, business profits) + indirect taxes net of subsidies + depreciation.
items.explanation: Plus a statistical discrepancy 'fudge factor' so the income and expenditure totals match.

items.prompt: The three main components of factor incomes are {{c1::wages and salaries}}, {{c2::interest}}, and {{c3::business profits (including rent)}}.
items.explanation: In 2023 wages were about 51% of Canadian GDP, interest and investment income about 9%, profits about 13%.

items.prompt: Why are indirect taxes added, and subsidies subtracted, when measuring GDP from the income side?
items.answer: Indirect taxes (on production and sale, e.g., GST) are part of the market price but go to government, not to factors; subsidies act like negative taxes, lowering market price below factor payments.
items.explanation: Factor incomes alone give *net domestic income at factor cost*; adding indirect taxes less subsidies and depreciation converts it to GDP at market prices.

items.prompt: **Depreciation** is the portion of current output that {{c1::replaces worn-out physical capital}}.
items.explanation: It is a non-factor payment: it is part of the value of output but is not income to any factor.

items.prompt: **Nominal GDP** is GDP valued at {{c1::current}} prices; **real GDP** is GDP valued at {{c2::base-period}} prices.
items.explanation: If nominal and real GDP change by different amounts, prices must have changed.

items.prompt: $\text{GDP deflator} = \dfrac{\text{Nominal GDP}}{{{c1::\text{Real GDP}}}} \times {{c2::100}}$
items.explanation: It is an index equal to 100 in the base year. Its change measures the average change in the price of all items in GDP.

items.prompt: $\text{Real GDP} = \dfrac{\text{Nominal GDP}}{{{c1::\text{GDP deflator}}}} \times 100$
items.explanation: Canada 2023: nominal \$2888.9b, deflator 122.9, so real GDP (2017 prices) $= 2888.9 / 122.9 \times 100 \approx 2351$ billion.

items.prompt: Year 1: 100 bushels of wheat at \$10 and 20 tonnes of steel at \$50. Year 2 prices: wheat \$12, steel \$55. Nominal GDP in year 1 and real GDP in year 1 at year-2 prices?
items.answer: Nominal: $100 \times 10 + 20 \times 50 = \$2000$. Real (year-2 prices): $100 \times 12 + 20 \times 55 = \$2300$.
items.explanation: Deflator for year 1 with year 2 as base: $\frac{2000}{2300} \times 100 = 86.96$. In the base year itself nominal = real and the deflator is 100.

items.prompt: In the base year, how do nominal GDP, real GDP and the GDP deflator compare?
items.answer: Nominal GDP equals real GDP and the deflator is exactly 100.
items.explanation: Canada's current base is 2017: nominal and real GDP were both \$2140.6 billion that year.

items.prompt: Nominal GDP rose 6% while the GDP deflator rose 4%. Roughly what happened to real GDP?
items.answer: Real GDP rose about 2% (approximately $6\% - 4\%$).
items.explanation: Growth of nominal $\approx$ growth of real + inflation. If prices rise faster than nominal GDP, real GDP actually falls.

items.prompt: GDP deflator vs CPI: what does each measure?
items.answer: **CPI**: the average price of goods and services bought by *consumers* (including imports). **GDP deflator**: the average price of goods and services *produced in Canada* (including exports and capital goods).
items.explanation: So they need not move together: a jump in the price of imported oil hits the CPI, while a jump in the price of exported lumber hits the deflator.

items.prompt: Growth rate of real GDP: $g = \dfrac{Y_t - Y_{t-1}}{{{c1::Y_{t-1}}}} \times 100$
items.explanation: Example: real GDP goes from 2000 to 2050, growth $= \frac{50}{2000} \times 100 = 2.5\%$.

items.prompt: Name the main kinds of economic activity omitted from official GDP.
items.answer: Illegal activities, the underground economy, home production/volunteering/leisure, and free digital products. GDP also fails to subtract economic 'bads' like pollution.
items.explanation: GDP measures the flow of activity in *organized markets*, so non-market activity is missed.

items.prompt: Is real per capita GDP a good measure of well-being?
items.answer: It is a good measure of *average material living standards* but an incomplete measure of overall well-being (leisure, environment, distribution are left out).

items.prompt: GDP vs GNP: what is the difference?
items.answer: **GDP** counts production within Canada's borders regardless of who owns the factors; **GNP** counts income earned by Canadian-owned factors wherever they are located.
items.explanation: GNP = GDP + net factor income from abroad. A US-owned plant in Ontario adds to Canadian GDP but its profits add to US GNP.

items.prompt: Desired expenditure vs actual expenditure: what is the notation difference and the meaning?
items.answer: Actual values carry a subscript $a$ ($C_a, I_a, G_a, X_a - IM_a$); desired (planned) values have no subscript ($C, I, G, X - IM$). Desired is what agents *would like* to buy given income and prices.
items.explanation: Desired is not unconstrained wishful spending; it already reflects real-world income and price constraints.

items.prompt: Desired aggregate expenditure: $AE = {{c1::C + I + G + (X - IM)}}$, the sum of desired spending by all four groups.
Expenditure that does *not* change systematically with national income is **{{c1::autonomous}}**; expenditure that does is **{{c2::induced}}**.
items.explanation: In the simplest model, investment is autonomous while consumption has an induced part ($MPC \times Y_D$) and an autonomous part (the intercept).

items.prompt: The *simplest* short-run macro model assumes no {{c1::government (so no taxes)}}, no {{c2::foreign sector (closed economy)}}, and a constant {{c3::price level}}.
$\text{Disposable income} = \text{Household income} - {{c1::\text{Taxes}}}$ and $\text{Saving} = \text{Disposable income} - {{c2::\text{Consumption}}}$.
items.explanation: Written $Y_D = Y - T$ and $S = Y_D - C$. With no government, $Y_D = Y$.

items.prompt: What determines desired consumption, according to the consumption function?
items.answer: Disposable income, wealth, interest rates and expectations about the future.
items.explanation: Disposable income moves consumption *along* the function; the other three *shift* it.

items.prompt: $APC = \dfrac{{{c1::C}}}{Y_D}$ (share of disposable income consumed) and $MPC = \dfrac{{{c2::\Delta C}}}{\Delta Y_D}$ (fraction of an extra dollar consumed).
items.explanation: The MPC is the constant slope of the consumption function; the APC starts infinitely large (positive consumption at zero income) and falls toward the MPC as $Y_D$ rises.

items.prompt: $APS = \dfrac{{{c1::S}}}{Y_D}$ and $MPS = \dfrac{{{c2::\Delta S}}}{\Delta Y_D}$; the MPS is the constant slope of the saving function.
items.explanation: The APS starts infinitely negative (dissaving at zero income) and rises toward the MPS as disposable income rises.

items.prompt: Because all disposable income is either spent or saved: $APC + APS = {{c1::1}}$ and $MPC + MPS = {{c2::1}}$.
items.explanation: If $MPC = 0.8$ then $MPS = 0.2$: of each extra dollar, 80 cents is consumed and 20 cents saved.

items.prompt: What shifts the consumption function **upward** (and the saving function downward)?
items.answer: An increase in wealth, a decrease in interest rates, or an increase in optimism about the future.
items.explanation: Each makes households want to consume more out of any given disposable income. The opposite changes shift it downward.

items.prompt: Consumption function $C = 30 + 0.8\,Y_D$. At $Y_D = 300$, what are $C$, $S$, the APC and the MPC?
items.explanation: $C = 30 + 240 = 270$; $S = 300 - 270 = 30$; $APC = 270/300 = 0.9$; the MPC is the slope, 0.8, at every income level. (Figure 6-3 plots exactly these points.)

items.prompt: What are the main determinants of desired investment expenditure?
items.answer: The real interest rate, changes in the level of sales, and business confidence.
items.explanation: A lower real interest rate, rising sales or more confidence all raise desired investment.

items.prompt: In the simple model, is investment autonomous or induced? Why?
items.answer: Autonomous: current real GDP is *not* a major determinant of current desired investment, so $I$ is treated as a constant (e.g., $I = 75$).

items.prompt: Which component of GDP is the most volatile and most associated with aggregate fluctuations?
items.answer: Investment expenditure.

items.prompt: With $C = 30 + 0.8Y$, $I = 75$, no government and no trade, what is the AE function?
items.explanation: With no taxes $Y_D = Y$, so the slides write the consumption function directly in $Y$. The intercept 105 is total autonomous expenditure; the slope 0.8 is the marginal propensity to spend.

items.prompt: The slope of the AE function is the **marginal propensity to spend**, which in the simplest model is just the {{c1::marginal propensity to consume (MPC)}}.
items.explanation: With no taxes and no imports, every extra dollar of income raises spending by the MPC.

items.prompt: Equilibrium national income occurs where desired aggregate expenditure equals actual national income: ${{c1::AE = Y}}$.
items.explanation: Graphically, where the AE function crosses the $45^\circ$ line.

items.prompt: If desired $AE$ exceeds actual income $Y$, what happens to inventories and output?
items.answer: Inventories are *falling* (unplanned decumulation), so firms raise production and $Y$ rises toward equilibrium.
items.explanation: If $AE < Y$, inventories pile up and firms cut production. Only at $AE = Y$ is there no pressure for output to change.

items.prompt: Solve for equilibrium income when $AE = 105 + 0.8Y$.
items.answer: $Y = 105 + 0.8Y \Rightarrow 0.2Y = 105 \Rightarrow Y = 525$
items.explanation: General form: $Y = \dfrac{A}{1 - z}$ with autonomous spending $A = 105$ and marginal propensity to spend $z = 0.8$. Figure 6-7 and Table 6-1 show $Y_0 = 525$: below it inventories fall and output rises, above it inventories pile up.

items.prompt: A parallel up-or-down move of the AE function is a **{{c1::shift}}** (change in autonomous expenditure); a change in its slope is a **{{c2::rotation}}** (change in the marginal propensity to spend).
The **simple multiplier** ($sm$) is the ratio of the change in equilibrium income to the change in autonomous expenditure that caused it: $sm = \dfrac{{{c1::\Delta Y}}}{{{c2::\Delta A}}}$.
items.explanation: 'Simple' because the price level is held constant. The slides abbreviate it $sm$.

items.prompt: $sm = \dfrac{\Delta Y}{\Delta A} = \dfrac{1}{{{c1::1 - z}}} > 1$, where $z$ is the marginal propensity to spend out of national income and $z < 1$.
items.explanation: With $z = 0.8$ the multiplier is $1/0.2 = 5$: a \$10 billion rise in investment raises equilibrium income by \$50 billion.

items.prompt: If the marginal propensity to spend rises, what happens to the slope of AE and to the simple multiplier?
items.answer: AE becomes steeper and the simple multiplier becomes larger.
items.explanation: $z = 0.5 \Rightarrow$ multiplier 2; $z = 0.9 \Rightarrow$ multiplier 10. More of each round of income is re-spent, so the chain of spending is longer.

items.prompt: How can expectations make economic fluctuations 'self-fulfilling prophecies'?
items.answer: If firms become optimistic they raise desired investment, AE shifts up, and through the multiplier national income rises, creating the healthy economy they expected.
items.explanation: The same mechanism works in reverse: pessimism cuts spending and produces the feared slump.

items.prompt: **Fiscal policy** is the use of the government's {{c1::tax and spending}} policies to achieve government objectives.
**Net tax revenue** is total tax revenue minus transfer payments: $T = {{c1::tY}}$, where $t$ is the {{c2::net tax rate}} (extra net tax revenue when $Y$ rises by \$1).
items.explanation: Transfers (EI, pensions) are negative taxes, so $T$ nets them out. With $t = 0.1$, a \$100 rise in GDP raises net taxes by \$10.

items.prompt: With a proportional net tax: $Y_D = Y - T = Y - tY = {{c1::(1 - t)Y}}$
items.explanation: Disposable income is what households keep after taxes and after receiving transfers. With $t = 0.1$, $Y_D = 0.9Y$.

items.prompt: Budget balance: $BB = {{c1::T - G}}$; positive is a **surplus**, negative is a **deficit**.
items.explanation: $T$ is *net* tax revenue (taxes minus transfers), so transfers reduce the balance even though they are not part of $G$.

items.prompt: With $C = 30 + 0.8\,Y_D$ and $t = 0.1$, write $C$ as a function of national income $Y$.
items.explanation: The MPC out of *disposable* income is still 0.8, but the marginal propensity to consume out of *national* income is $0.8 \times 0.9 = 0.72$.

items.prompt: Why are exports $X$ treated as autonomous in the model?
items.answer: Exports depend on decisions of *foreign* households and firms, so they do not change systematically with Canadian national income.

items.prompt: The **marginal propensity to import** ($m$) is the rise in imports induced by a \$1 rise in national income, so the import function is $M = {{c1::mY}}$.
items.explanation: Imports are *induced*: as Canadians earn more, they buy more foreign goods. The Ch. 7 formula slides write imports as $M$; the Ch. 5–6 slides and the figures write $IM$ (same thing).

items.prompt: Net export function: $NX = X - M = {{c1::X - mY}}$, which is {{c2::negatively}} related to national income.
items.explanation: Its slope is $-m$: $X$ is flat while imports rise with $Y$.

items.prompt: Foreign income rises. What happens to the $X$ and $NX$ functions?
items.answer: Both shift **upward**, parallel to their original position (foreigners buy more Canadian goods at every level of Canadian income).

items.prompt: Canadian prices rise relative to foreign prices. What happens to exports, the import function and $NX$?
items.answer: $X$ shifts **down**; $m$ rises so the import function **rotates up**; $NX$ shifts **downward** at every level of income.
items.explanation: Canadian goods are now relatively expensive both for foreigners and for Canadians choosing between domestic and foreign goods.

items.prompt: The Canadian dollar depreciates. Effect on net exports?
items.answer: $NX$ rises: foreigners pay less of their currency for one C\$ (Canadian goods cheaper abroad, $X$ up) and Canadians pay more C\$ for foreign currency (imports dearer, $IM$ down).
items.explanation: Exchange-rate changes are the most important cause of changes in international relative prices.

items.prompt: Full AE function: $AE = C + I + G + X - M$, whose slope is $z$, the {{c1::marginal propensity to spend out of national income}}.
With government and trade, the marginal propensity to spend is $z = {{c1::(1 - t)c - m}}$, where $c$ is the MPC.
items.explanation: Of each extra dollar of income, $(1 - t)$ survives net taxes, a fraction $c$ of that is consumed, and $m$ leaks abroad as imports. In a closed economy with no government, $z = c$.

items.prompt: The slides' Canadian calibration: $c = 0.80$, $t = 0.25$, $m = 0.35$. Compute $z$ and the simple multiplier $sm$.
items.explanation: Compare the closed no-government economy with $c = 0.8$: $sm = 1/0.2 = 5$. Taxes and imports cut the Canadian multiplier to about 1.3.

items.prompt: Figure 7-3: $C = 30 + 0.72Y$, $I = 75$, $G = 51$, $NX = 72 - 0.1Y$. Write the AE function and find equilibrium income.
Why do taxes and imports reduce the simple multiplier?
items.answer: They are *leakages*: each round of extra income loses $t$ to net taxes and $m$ to imports, so $z = (1 - t)c - m$ is smaller and $\frac{1}{1 - z}$ is smaller.
items.explanation: Closed economy, no government: $z = c = 0.8$, $sm = 5$. Canada with $t = 0.25$, $m = 0.35$: $z = 0.25$, $sm \approx 1.3$.

items.prompt: All else equal, the simple multiplier $sm$ is **larger** when which parameters move which way?
items.answer: When $c$ (the MPC) rises, when $t$ falls, or when $m$ falls.
items.explanation: Each raises $z = (1 - t)c - m$.

items.prompt: Exports rise by \$1 billion. By how much does equilibrium national income change?
items.answer: By \$1 billion times the simple multiplier, because $X$ is autonomous.

items.prompt: What two fiscal policy tools does the government have in this model, and how do they raise equilibrium income?
items.answer: **Government purchases** $G$ (an increase *shifts* AE up) and the **net tax rate** $t$ (a reduction *rotates* AE steeper, raising $z$).
items.explanation: Both set the multiplier process in motion. Stabilization policy aims to reduce cyclical fluctuations in national income.

items.prompt: Government purchases rise by $\Delta G$: $\Delta Y = \Delta G \times sm = \dfrac{\Delta G}{{{c1::1 - z}}}$
items.explanation: With the Canadian $z = 0.25$ ($sm \approx 1.3$), \$10 billion of extra purchases raises equilibrium income by about \$13 billion.

items.prompt: Why does a rise in the price level reduce desired consumption?
items.answer: Much private wealth is held in assets with fixed nominal value (e.g., money); a higher price level lowers their real value, so autonomous consumption falls and AE shifts down.
items.explanation: Bonds do not matter here: a price-level change hurts bondholders and helps bond issuers by equal amounts, leaving aggregate wealth unchanged.

items.prompt: Why does a rise in the domestic price level (exchange rate unchanged) reduce net exports?
items.answer: Canadian goods become relatively more expensive, so Canadians and foreigners buy fewer Canadian-made goods and more foreign ones: $NX$ and AE shift down.

items.prompt: The **aggregate demand (AD) curve** shows combinations of {{c1::real GDP}} and the {{c2::price level}} for which desired aggregate expenditure equals actual national income.
items.explanation: Every point on AD is an $AE = Y$ equilibrium for some price level; AD is derived by varying $P$ and tracing the resulting equilibrium $Y$.

items.prompt: A change in the price level causes what for the AE curve, and what for the AD curve?
items.answer: A **shift** of the AE curve but a **movement along** the AD curve.
items.explanation: Rising $P$ shifts AE down and moves the economy up and to the left along AD (lower equilibrium GDP). This shift-vs-movement distinction is a favourite exam trap.

items.prompt: What shifts the AD curve?
items.answer: Anything that shifts the AE curve *other than a price-level change*: a change in autonomous expenditure ($C$, $I$, $G$, $X$, or a tax change). Such shifts are called aggregate demand shocks.
items.explanation: A rise in autonomous spending shifts AE up and AD to the **right**; a fall shifts AD to the left.

items.prompt: The horizontal shift of the AD curve from a change in autonomous expenditure equals the {{c1::simple multiplier}} times the change in autonomous expenditure.
items.explanation: The simple multiplier holds the price level fixed, which is exactly what a horizontal shift (same $P$) measures.

items.prompt: The **aggregate supply (AS) curve** shows the relation between the price level and the quantity of output supplied, for given {{c1::technology}} and {{c2::factor prices}}.
Why does the AS curve slope upward?
items.answer: As output rises, unit costs rise: less efficient standby plants are used, less efficient workers hired, and overtime is paid. Firms need a higher price to supply more.
items.explanation: AS gets *steeper* at higher output because unit costs rise faster as capacity is approached.

items.prompt: A rise in factor prices (wages, oil) shifts the AS curve {{c1::leftward (upward)}}; a fall in factor prices shifts it {{c2::rightward}}.
items.explanation: Each unit now costs more to produce, so firms require a higher price for any given output.

items.prompt: Technology improves. Which way does AS shift?
items.answer: **Rightward**: unit costs fall, so more is supplied at every price level.
items.explanation: A deterioration in technology shifts AS leftward. Shifts of AS from exogenous forces are called aggregate supply shocks.

items.prompt: **Macroeconomic equilibrium** is at the intersection of the {{c1::AD and AS}} curves and determines both {{c2::real GDP and the price level}}.
How are 'positive' and 'negative' AD/AS shocks defined?
items.answer: By their effect on real GDP: positive shocks *increase* equilibrium GDP, negative shocks *reduce* it.
items.explanation: So a negative AS shock (AS shifts left) is 'negative' because $Y$ falls, even though $P$ rises.

items.prompt: Aggregate **demand** shocks move the price level and real GDP in the {{c1::same}} direction; aggregate **supply** shocks move them in {{c2::opposite}} directions.
items.explanation: AD up: $P \uparrow$, $Y \uparrow$. Negative AS shock (AS left): $P \uparrow$, $Y \downarrow$, i.e., stagflation; the rise in $P$ also shifts AE down.

items.prompt: When the price level can vary, is the effect of a rise in autonomous expenditure on real GDP larger or smaller than the simple multiplier predicts? Why?
items.answer: Smaller. The AE curve shifts up, but the resulting rise in the price level shifts it part of the way back down.
items.explanation: The effect of an AD shift is split between a change in $Y$ and a change in $P$; the simple multiplier gives only the horizontal shift of AD.

items.prompt: How does the steepness of the AS curve change the split of an AD shift between output and prices?
items.answer: The steeper the AS curve, the greater the price effect and the smaller the output effect.
items.explanation: Near capacity AS is steep, so demand stimulus mostly raises prices; with lots of slack AS is flat, so it mostly raises output.

items.prompt: How do the slides analyze the 2020 COVID recession in the AD/AS model?
items.answer: A large leftward AS shift (firms could not combine inputs safely) *and* a large leftward AD shift (households and firms cut demand even at unchanged income); both cut real GDP sharply.
items.explanation: Both shocks reversed relatively quickly once vaccines allowed workplaces and businesses to reopen in 2021.

items.prompt: What are the two key assumptions of the macro model in the **short run**?
items.answer: Factor prices are exogenous (changes are not explained within the model); technology and factor supplies, hence $Y^*$, are constant.
items.explanation: In this state real GDP is determined by AD and AS; we study it to see the effects of shocks.

items.prompt: What are the assumptions of the **adjustment process** state?
items.answer: Factor prices adjust (are endogenous) in response to output gaps; technology and factor supplies, hence $Y^*$, are still constant.
items.explanation: Real GDP eventually returns to $Y^*$. We study it to see why output gaps are temporary.

items.prompt: What are the assumptions of the **long run**, and what happens there?
items.answer: Factor prices have fully adjusted to any output gap, and technology and factor supplies are changing. Potential GDP $Y^*$ grows over time.
items.explanation: Studied to understand long-run economic growth (Chapter 10).

items.prompt: Output is above potential ($Y > Y^*$). What happens to wages and why?
items.answer: Wages **rise**: firms producing beyond normal capacity face excess demand for labour and other factors, workers have bargaining power, and profits are high.
items.explanation: Higher wages raise unit costs, shifting AS leftward until $Y$ falls back to $Y^*$ at a higher price level.

items.prompt: Output is below potential ($Y < Y^*$). What happens to wages and why?
items.answer: Wages tend to **fall** (slowly): there is excess supply of labour, firms have below-normal sales and low profits, so they resist raises and even seek cuts.
items.explanation: Lower unit costs shift AS rightward, raising $Y$ back toward $Y^*$ at a lower price level.

items.prompt: What is downward wage stickiness, and what asymmetry does it create?
items.answer: Wages rise rapidly in booms but fall only slowly in recessions, so inflationary gaps close quickly while recessionary gaps can persist for a long time.

items.prompt: The **Phillips curve** is the {{c1::negative}} relationship between the unemployment rate and the rate of change of {{c2::wages}}, observed by A.W. Phillips.
items.explanation: Wages tend to fall when unemployment is high and rise when it is low, which is the labour-market side of the factor-price adjustment story.

items.prompt: In what sense is potential output an 'anchor' for the economy?
items.answer: After any AD or AS shock, output gaps cause wages and other factor prices to adjust until equilibrium output returns to $Y^*$.

items.prompt: Trace a positive AD shock through the adjustment process.
items.answer: Short run: $Y$ rises above $Y^*$ and $P$ rises. Adjustment: the inflationary gap pushes wages up, AS shifts left, $Y$ returns to $Y^*$ and $P$ rises further.
items.explanation: Long-run result: no change in output, a higher price level.

items.prompt: Trace a negative AD shock through the adjustment process.
items.answer: Short run: $Y$ falls below $Y^*$ and $P$ falls. Adjustment: the recessionary gap (slowly) pushes wages down, AS shifts right, $Y$ returns to $Y^*$ at an even lower $P$.
items.explanation: Because of downward wage stickiness, this recovery can be slow, which is the case for fiscal stabilization.

items.prompt: Trace a negative AS shock (e.g., oil price jump) through the adjustment process.
items.answer: Short run: AS shifts left, $Y$ falls below $Y^*$ and $P$ rises. Adjustment: the recessionary gap pushes wages down, AS shifts back right, and $Y$ returns to $Y^*$ with $P$ back near its original level.

items.prompt: The economy is in **long-run equilibrium** when the AD and AS curves intersect at potential output $Y^*$, i.e., when there is {{c1::no output gap}} left for factor prices to respond to.
In the long run, what does a shift in the AD curve change: real GDP, the price level, or both?
items.answer: Only the price level. Real GDP returns to $Y^*$, so AD shifts have no long-run effect on output.
items.explanation: Fiscal or monetary stimulus therefore raises output only temporarily in this framework.

items.prompt: In the long run, an increase in potential output $Y^*$ does what to real GDP and the price level?
items.answer: Raises real GDP and **lowers** the price level.
items.explanation: More capacity shifts AS right along a given AD curve.

items.prompt: How does fiscal policy close a recessionary gap, and what happens to the price level?
items.answer: Raise $G$ or cut $t$ to shift AD rightward until $Y = Y^*$; the price level rises compared with waiting for wages to fall.
items.explanation: To close an *inflationary* gap, do the reverse: cut $G$ or raise $t$ to shift AD left, avoiding the wage-driven rise in prices.

items.prompt: What is the paradox of thrift, and in which run does it hold?
items.answer: An increase in saving (lower desired consumption) reduces real GDP. It holds only in the **short run**; in the long run higher saving raises investment and potential output.
items.explanation: In the long run output is pinned to $Y^*$, so more saving means more investment rather than less output.

items.prompt: How does the tax-and-transfer system act as an automatic stabilizer?
items.answer: When GDP rises, net tax revenue rises automatically (more taxes, fewer transfers), dampening the rise; when GDP falls the reverse. No policy decision is needed.
items.explanation: Mechanically, a higher $t$ lowers $z = (1 - t)c - m$ and thus the simple multiplier $1/(1 - z)$.

items.prompt: A lower net tax rate $t$ makes the simple multiplier larger or smaller, and real GDP more or less stable?
items.answer: Larger multiplier, and real GDP is **less stable** in response to shocks to autonomous spending.

items.prompt: The **decision lag** is the time between {{c1::perceiving a problem and deciding what to do}}; the **execution lag** is the time to {{c2::put the policy in place after the decision}}.
items.explanation: Both limit discretionary fiscal policy: by the time stimulus arrives, the gap may have closed on its own.

items.prompt: **{{c1::Fine tuning}}** tries to keep output at potential with frequent policy changes; **{{c2::gross tuning}}** only tries to ensure output gaps do not persist for long.
items.explanation: Most economists favour gross tuning because of lags and uncertainty.

items.prompt: Do temporary or permanent tax changes have the bigger effect on aggregate demand?
items.answer: Permanent changes. Temporary tax changes generally have less impact on AD because forward-looking households smooth consumption.

items.prompt: What is crowding out, and when is its negative effect reduced?
items.answer: Government spending displacing private investment. The damage is smaller if the extra government purchases themselves raise potential output or its growth rate (e.g., infrastructure).
items.explanation: Tax-rate cuts give short-run demand stimulus and may also raise the level and growth rate of $Y^*$.

items.prompt: Why do small differences in growth rates matter so much?
items.answer: Growth compounds: \$100 growing at 2% per year becomes about \$725 after 100 years, but at 3% it becomes about \$1922.
items.explanation: Over a few decades, a one-point difference in the growth rate makes an enormous difference in the *level* of income.

items.prompt: Rule of 70: how long does it take income to double at growth rate $g$ percent per year?
items.answer: About $70 / g$ years. At 2% roughly 35 years; at 7% roughly 10 years.
items.explanation: Check against Table 10-1: at 7%, \$100 becomes \$197 after 10 years.

items.prompt: What are the main benefits of economic growth listed in the course?
items.answer: Rising average material living standards (shifting consumption toward services, funding demand for a cleaner environment) and the resources to address poverty and inequality.
items.explanation: Caveat: in recent decades much aggregate income growth in Canada has accrued to top earners, so inequality has risen alongside average income.

items.prompt: What are the two costs of economic growth?
items.answer: **Forgone consumption** (investing for future output means consuming less today) and **social costs** (disruption to businesses and workers whose skills become obsolete).

items.prompt: Four major sources of growth in potential GDP: growth in the {{c1::labour force}}, growth in {{c2::human capital}}, growth in {{c3::physical capital}}, and {{c4::technological improvement}}.
items.explanation: Different growth theories emphasize different sources: the Neoclassical model stresses capital and (exogenous) technology, newer theories stress endogenous technology.

items.prompt: How does the long-run version of the model differ from the short-run version in how saving equals investment?
items.answer: Short run: real GDP adjusts until desired saving equals desired investment. Long run: real GDP is fixed at $Y^*$ and the **real interest rate** adjusts to equate them.

items.prompt: Desired **private saving** at $Y^*$: $S_{PVT} = {{c1::Y^* - T - C}}$ (income left after taxes and consumption).
**Public saving** is the combined budget balance of all levels of government: $S_{GOV} = {{c1::T - G}}$.
items.explanation: A budget deficit is negative public saving.

items.prompt: **National saving** $NS = S_{PVT} + S_{GOV} = Y^* - T - C + T - G = {{c1::Y^* - C - G}}$
items.explanation: Taxes cancel out: for a given $Y^*$, national saving falls if either households consume more or the government purchases more.

items.prompt: The supply of national saving increases. Effect on the real interest rate, investment and the growth of potential output?
items.answer: The real interest rate **falls**, investment **rises**, and potential output grows **faster**.
items.explanation: More saving means more funds offered to firms at every interest rate; the price of funds falls and more projects become profitable.

items.prompt: Investment demand increases (e.g., new technology makes projects profitable). Effect on the real interest rate, saving and growth?
items.answer: The real interest rate **rises**, which encourages more saving; the higher rate of saving and investment raises the growth rate of potential output.

items.prompt: Aggregate production function: $GDP = F_\theta({{c1::L, K, H}})$, where $L$ is labour, $K$ physical capital, $H$ human capital and $\theta$ the state of technology.
items.explanation: For simplicity the course combines $K$ and $H$ into a single 'capital' and holds technology constant.

items.prompt: The Neoclassical production function has **{{c1::diminishing marginal returns}}** when one factor increases on its own and **{{c2::constant returns to scale}}** when all factors increase together.
In the Neoclassical model, what happens when the labour force grows with fixed capital?
items.answer: GDP rises, but because of diminishing marginal returns output per person eventually **falls**: material living standards decline.

items.prompt: In the Neoclassical model, what does capital accumulation do to living standards?
items.answer: It raises output per worker and living standards, but each additional increment of capital gives a smaller improvement (diminishing returns).

items.prompt: Capital and labour grow at the same rate with constant technology. What happens to GDP and to per capita output?
items.answer: GDP rises (constant returns to scale), but per capita output does **not** change, so living standards do not improve.
items.explanation: Balanced growth without technical change cannot raise living standards; this is why technology is the key to sustained growth in the model.

items.prompt: How is technological change treated in the Neoclassical model, and what can it do?
items.answer: It is **exogenous** (unexplained by the model) and can raise potential output even without capital accumulation or labour-force growth.

items.prompt: **Embodied technical change** is technological change due to improvements in the {{c1::quality of new capital goods}}.
items.explanation: Much new technology enters the economy only when firms buy new machines, so investment and technical change are linked.

items.prompt: Why might high immigration fail to raise Canadian per-capita income, according to the slides?
items.answer: Immigrants may enter at below-average wages, immigration may hold wages down, and it can stretch 'absorptive capacity' (housing, classrooms, doctors, infrastructure).
items.explanation: Economists see labour shortages as short-run problems that higher wages fix; immigration is not bad but needs to be paced and designed carefully.

items.prompt: What does it mean that technological change is **endogenous**?
items.answer: It responds to economic signals (prices and profits) and results from costly, risky, innovative activity inside the economic system, rather than arriving from outside.
items.explanation: Channels: learning by doing, knowledge transfer, market structure and innovation, and shocks that spur innovation.

items.prompt: What two sources of *increasing* returns challenge the Neoclassical assumption of diminishing returns to capital?
items.answer: **Market-development costs** (fixed costs of opening a market are paid once) and the **economics of ideas** (knowledge can be reused at no extra cost).

items.prompt: Do most economists think there are absolute limits to growth from resource exhaustion?
items.answer: No: limits based on constant technology and fixed resources are not relevant because technology and known resource stocks change continually, raising resource efficiency.
items.explanation: The real constraint is that further growth must be *sustainable*, driven by knowledge-based technological change.

items.prompt: According to the slides, what is the most effective policy to cut greenhouse-gas emissions?
items.answer: Putting a higher cost on emissions through a **carbon tax** or a **cap-and-trade** system.
items.explanation: Canada aims for net-zero emissions by 2050; once the economy adjusts to cleaner, more efficient energy, growth could even accelerate.

items.prompt: The three functions of money: {{c1::medium of exchange}}, {{c2::store of value}}, and {{c3::unit of account}}.
items.explanation: Medium of exchange removes the 'double coincidence of wants' problem of barter; high inflation damages the store-of-value function.

items.prompt: What is fiat money?
items.answer: Money that is not convertible into anything of intrinsic value and is accepted because the government declares it legal tender and people trust it will be accepted.
items.explanation: Canadian bank notes are fiat money; their value rests on confidence, not on gold backing.

items.prompt: Roughly, what is in M1 and what does M2 add?
items.answer: **M1** (narrow money): currency outside banks plus chequable (demand) deposits. **M2** adds less liquid deposits such as savings/notice deposits and personal term deposits.
items.explanation: Which measure is 'money' is a matter of degree of liquidity; credit cards are not money (they create a debt).

items.prompt: What are the main functions of the Bank of Canada?
items.answer: Banker to the commercial banks, banker to the federal government, regulator of the money supply (monetary policy), and supporter/regulator of financial markets.
items.explanation: It is a Crown corporation whose Governor is appointed for a seven-year term; it operates with day-to-day independence from the government.

items.prompt: Quantity theory of money: $MV = {{c1::PY}}$, where $V$ is the velocity of circulation.
items.explanation: If $V$ and $Y$ are constant, the price level is proportional to the money supply: sustained inflation requires sustained money growth.

items.prompt: In a **fractional-reserve** system, banks hold only a fraction of their deposits as {{c1::reserves}} and lend out the rest.
items.explanation: Reserves are cash in the vault plus deposits at the Bank of Canada. Canada has no legal minimum; banks choose a *target* reserve ratio.

items.prompt: $\text{Reserve ratio} = \dfrac{{{c1::\text{Reserves}}}}{\text{Deposits}}$; **excess reserves** are reserves above the bank's target.
With target reserve ratio $v$ and no cash drain, a new deposit of $\Delta R$ raises total deposits by $\Delta D = \dfrac{\Delta R}{{{c1::v}}}$; the money multiplier is $1/v$.
items.explanation: $v = 0.1$: a \$1000 new deposit lets the bank lend \$900, which is redeposited and relent (\$810, \$729, ...), summing to \$10,000.

items.prompt: How does a cash drain $c$ (fraction of new deposits the public holds as currency) change the money multiplier?
items.answer: It shrinks it to $\dfrac{1}{v + c}$. Example: $v = 0.1$, $c = 0.1$ gives 5 instead of 10.
items.explanation: Cash held outside banks cannot be relent, so each round of deposit creation is smaller.

items.prompt: Why would banks holding excess reserves reduce the money multiplier?
items.answer: Money is created only when banks *lend* excess reserves; if they keep them (e.g., in a crisis), fewer deposits are created and the actual multiplier is below $1/v$.

items.prompt: Target reserve ratio 20%, no cash drain. A \$500 cash deposit eventually raises the money supply by how much?
items.answer: Deposits rise by $500 / 0.2 = \$2500$; since \$500 of currency moved into the bank, the money supply rises by \$2000.
items.explanation: Classic trap: the first deposit converts currency (already money) into a deposit; only the \$2000 of new loans is new money.

items.prompt: Bond prices and interest rates: what is the relationship?
items.answer: **Inverse**: a bond's price is the present value of its fixed future payments, so a higher interest rate lowers the price, and vice versa.
items.explanation: A bond paying \$100 in one year is worth $100/1.05 \approx \$95.24$ at 5% but $100/1.10 \approx \$90.91$ at 10%.

items.prompt: Present value of \$R received in one year at interest rate $i$: $PV = \dfrac{R}{{{c1::1 + i}}}$
items.explanation: For $n$ years, divide by $(1 + i)^n$. The higher $i$, the lower the PV: money later is worth less today.

items.prompt: Three motives for holding money: the **{{c1::transactions}}** motive (bridging receipts and payments), the **{{c2::precautionary}}** motive (unexpected needs), and the **{{c3::speculative}}** motive (avoiding capital losses on bonds).
How does the quantity of money demanded respond to the interest rate, real income and the price level?
items.answer: Negatively to the interest rate (the opportunity cost of holding money), positively to real GDP and positively to the price level.
items.explanation: The money demand curve slopes down against $i$; higher $Y$ or $P$ shifts it right.

items.prompt: Money supply exceeds money demand at the current interest rate. What happens?
items.answer: People use excess money to buy bonds, bond prices rise and the interest rate **falls** until money demanded equals the (fixed) money supply.
items.explanation: Monetary equilibrium: the interest rate is determined where money supply equals money demand (liquidity preference).

items.prompt: State the monetary transmission mechanism for an increase in the money supply.
items.answer: $M_S \uparrow \Rightarrow i \downarrow \Rightarrow$ desired investment (and other interest-sensitive spending) $\uparrow \Rightarrow AE \uparrow \Rightarrow AD$ shifts right $\Rightarrow Y \uparrow$, $P \uparrow$.
items.explanation: In an open economy the lower interest rate also causes a capital outflow, a depreciation of the C\$ and higher net exports, reinforcing the effect.

items.prompt: How does the exchange-rate channel of monetary transmission work when Canadian interest rates fall?
items.answer: Lower rates make Canadian assets less attractive, capital flows out, the C\$ depreciates, exports rise and imports fall, so $NX$ and AD rise.

items.prompt: When is monetary policy most powerful (largest effect on AD)?
items.answer: When money demand is insensitive to the interest rate (steep $M_D$, so a given $M_S$ change moves $i$ a lot) and investment is very sensitive to the interest rate (flat $I$ curve).
items.explanation: The opposite combination (flat $M_D$, steep $I$) makes monetary policy weak; this was the Keynesian vs monetarist debate.

items.prompt: Long-run effect of a one-time increase in the money supply on output and prices?
items.answer: Output returns to $Y^*$ through factor-price adjustment; the price level ends permanently higher (money is neutral in the long run).

items.prompt: Since 1991 the Bank of Canada has targeted CPI inflation at {{c1::2}}% (the midpoint of a {{c2::1–3}}% band), under an agreement with the federal government renewed roughly every five years.
items.explanation: The target is for total CPI inflation, but the Bank watches *core* inflation measures that strip out volatile components as a guide to the trend.

items.prompt: The Bank of Canada's policy instrument is the target for the {{c1::overnight interest rate}}, the rate at which major financial institutions lend to each other overnight.
items.explanation: The Bank announces the target on eight fixed dates per year; changes feed through to other market rates such as the prime rate.

items.prompt: How does the bank rate relate to the overnight target?
items.answer: The bank rate (what the Bank charges banks for short-term loans) sits at the top of the operating band around the overnight target, so it moves one-for-one with the target.

items.prompt: Inflation is forecast to rise above target because of an inflationary gap. What does the Bank of Canada do and why?
items.answer: It **raises** the overnight target: higher interest rates reduce interest-sensitive spending and appreciate the C\$, shifting AD left and closing the gap.
items.explanation: A recessionary gap with inflation below target calls for the opposite: cut the target rate.

items.prompt: How long do changes in Canadian monetary policy take to have their full effect on inflation, and what does this imply?
items.answer: Roughly 18 to 24 months. The Bank must act on *forecast* inflation, not current inflation, and policy mistakes are hard to reverse quickly.

items.prompt: When the Bank targets an interest rate, is the money supply exogenous or endogenous?
items.answer: Endogenous: the Bank supplies whatever quantity of money is demanded at the targeted rate, so the money supply adjusts to money demand.
items.explanation: This reverses the textbook sequence 'choose $M_S$, let $i$ adjust'; in practice the Bank chooses $i$ and $M_S$ follows.

items.prompt: Demand inflation vs supply inflation?
items.answer: **Demand (demand-pull)**: AD shifts right, creating an inflationary gap that pushes wages and prices up. **Supply (cost-push)**: AS shifts left (e.g., oil shock), raising prices while output falls.
items.explanation: Demand inflation: $P \uparrow$, $Y \uparrow$. Supply inflation: $P \uparrow$, $Y \downarrow$ (stagflation).

items.prompt: What two forces drive wage changes in the course's inflation model?
items.answer: The **output gap** (excess demand for labour raises wages, excess supply lowers them) and **expected inflation** (workers and firms build expected price rises into wage settlements).
items.explanation: Actual inflation $\approx$ expected inflation + output-gap effect (+ supply shocks).

items.prompt: What does it mean for the Bank of Canada to 'validate' an inflationary gap?
items.answer: To increase the money supply (keep rates low) so AD keeps shifting right as AS shifts left; output stays above $Y^*$ and inflation continues instead of the gap closing.

items.prompt: Can inflation be sustained indefinitely without monetary validation?
items.answer: No. Without money growth, a leftward-shifting AS eventually closes the inflationary gap and inflation stops; sustained inflation requires sustained monetary expansion.
items.explanation: Hence the saying that sustained inflation is 'always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon'.

items.prompt: Why does holding output above $Y^*$ with continued validation lead to *accelerating* inflation?
items.answer: Inflation expectations keep rising to match actual inflation, so wages rise by expectations plus the gap effect; keeping the gap open requires ever-faster money growth.
items.explanation: This is the acceleration hypothesis: a persistent inflationary gap cannot buy a stable positive inflation rate.

items.prompt: After a negative supply shock, what are the Bank's two options and their consequences?
items.answer: **Validate** (expand money): output recovers faster but the price level rises further. **Don't validate**: a recessionary gap slowly pushes wages down and prices back, at the cost of a longer slump.

items.prompt: Describe the three phases of disinflation after a sustained inflation.
items.answer: (1) Remove validation: AD growth stops, but wages still rise from expectations, so a recessionary gap opens (stagflation). (2) Expectations fall, wages slow, output recovers. (3) Gap closes at a lower inflation rate.

items.prompt: The **sacrifice ratio** is the cumulative percentage-point loss of {{c1::output (GDP)}} per percentage-point reduction in {{c2::inflation}}.
items.explanation: It is smaller when expectations adjust quickly, e.g., when the central bank's commitment is credible.

items.prompt: The **NAIRU** (non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment) is the unemployment rate when $Y = {{c1::Y^*}}$; it equals frictional plus {{c2::structural}} unemployment.
items.explanation: Also called the natural rate. Below it, an inflationary gap makes inflation accelerate; above it, cyclical unemployment exists.

items.prompt: Cyclical unemployment $= u - {{c1::u^*}}$ (actual rate minus the NAIRU); it is {{c2::positive}} in a recessionary gap and negative in an inflationary gap.
A laid-off auto worker in Ontario cannot find work because new jobs are in Alberta's oil sector. Frictional or structural?
items.answer: **Structural**: a mismatch of location/skills between workers and jobs. Frictional would be a short search between similar jobs.

items.prompt: What kinds of changes raise the NAIRU?
items.answer: More generous or longer EI benefits, higher minimum wages above market levels, faster structural change (skill mismatch), and demographic shifts toward groups with higher turnover.
items.explanation: Policies that improve matching (training, job information, mobility) lower it.

items.prompt: Why might real wages not fall to clear the labour market in a recession (New Keynesian view)?
items.answer: Long-term wage contracts, efficiency wages (paying above market to boost effort and retention), menu costs of changing prices, and the insider-outsider bargaining of existing employees.

items.prompt: What is hysteresis in unemployment?
items.answer: A long recession raises the NAIRU itself: the long-term unemployed lose skills and contacts, so cyclical unemployment turns into structural unemployment.

items.prompt: A discouraged worker stops looking for a job. What happens to the measured unemployment rate and the participation rate?
items.answer: Both **fall**: the person leaves the labour force, so they are no longer counted as unemployed and the labour force shrinks.
items.explanation: The measured unemployment rate can therefore understate labour-market weakness.

items.prompt: Government budget deficit $= G + {{c1::iD}} - T$: purchases plus interest on the outstanding debt $D$, minus net tax revenue.
items.explanation: The **primary deficit** is $G - T$, excluding interest payments; it shows whether current programs are paid for by current taxes.

items.prompt: The **deficit** is a {{c1::flow}} (this year's excess of spending over revenue); the **debt** is a {{c2::stock}} (accumulated past deficits minus surpluses), so $\Delta D = \text{deficit}$.
Change in the debt-to-GDP ratio: $\Delta d = (r - g)\,d + {{c1::\text{primary deficit ratio}}}$, where $r$ is the real interest rate and $g$ real GDP growth.
items.explanation: If $r > g$ the ratio rises even with a balanced primary budget; if $g > r$ the economy can 'grow out of' the debt.

items.prompt: What is the cyclically adjusted (structural) deficit?
items.answer: The deficit that would exist if the economy were at potential output $Y^*$. It removes the automatic-stabilizer effects of the business cycle to show the stance of fiscal policy.
items.explanation: A deficit during a recession may be entirely cyclical; a deficit at $Y^*$ signals structural imbalance.

items.prompt: How do persistent deficits crowd out private investment in the long run?
items.answer: Deficits reduce national saving ($T - G$ falls), which raises the real interest rate in the market for financial capital and lowers investment, slowing growth of $Y^*$.
items.explanation: In an open economy the higher rate attracts foreign capital instead, appreciating the C\$ and crowding out net exports.

items.prompt: Why is an annually balanced budget rule destabilizing?
items.answer: In a recession tax revenue falls, so the rule forces spending cuts or tax hikes that shift AD further left; it disables the automatic stabilizers.
items.explanation: A budget balanced over the business cycle keeps stabilizers while limiting debt growth.

items.prompt: The balance of payments has the **{{c1::current account}}** (trade in goods and services, investment income, transfers) and the **{{c2::capital and financial account}}** (purchases and sales of assets), plus changes in official reserves.
Why must the balance of payments always sum to zero?
items.answer: Every transaction is recorded twice: a current-account deficit must be financed by net capital inflows (selling assets to foreigners) or by a fall in official reserves.
items.explanation: So 'a balance of payments deficit' in headlines usually means a current-account deficit.

items.prompt: Canada runs a current-account deficit. What does this imply for the capital and financial account?
items.answer: A matching surplus: Canada is a net borrower, selling more assets (bonds, shares, real estate) to foreigners than it buys abroad.

items.prompt: Who demands Canadian dollars in the foreign-exchange market?
items.answer: Foreigners buying Canadian exports, foreigners buying Canadian assets (capital inflows), and anyone paying Canadians income or transfers.
items.explanation: Supply of C\$ comes from Canadians buying imports or foreign assets.

items.prompt: Canadian inflation runs persistently above US inflation. Long-run effect on the C\$?
items.answer: The C\$ **depreciates** (exchange rate rises) roughly in line with the inflation differential, keeping relative prices (purchasing power parity) constant.

items.prompt: **Purchasing power parity** holds when the exchange rate adjusts so that a given amount of money buys the same {{c1::basket of goods}} in each country.
items.explanation: Prediction: the currency of the higher-inflation country depreciates. PPP works poorly in the short run because of capital flows and non-traded goods.

items.prompt: Canadian interest rates rise relative to US rates. Short-run effect on the C\$?
items.answer: Capital flows into Canadian assets, demand for C\$ rises and the C\$ **appreciates** (exchange rate falls).

items.prompt: World prices of Canada's commodity exports (oil, lumber) rise. Effect on the C\$?
items.answer: Export revenues rise, foreigners need more C\$, and the C\$ **appreciates**; this is why the C\$ is often called a commodity currency.

items.prompt: Fixed vs flexible exchange rate: how is each maintained?
items.answer: **Flexible**: the rate is set by supply and demand with no intervention (Canada). **Fixed**: the central bank buys or sells foreign reserves to hold the rate, and loses control of monetary policy.
